echoes.note: Mary's pure nard whose fragrance fills the house echoes the Song's 'while the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance.' The shared lexeme nardos (LXX) plus the banquet-couch setting and the diffusing scent give real Volume and Coherence; John frames the anointing of the messianic 'king' (the next pericope's title) in the idiom of the Bride's love-gift.

The catalogue of spices 'nard and saffron... with all chief spices' supplies the only other biblical concentration of nard as a costly love-perfume, reinforcing the Songs register behind Mary's extravagant anointing. Low confidence: thematic resonance without verbal anchor beyond the shared spice.

Anointing with oil is the act that makes a king/Messiah (christos); Mary's anointing of Jesus figurally enacts the royal-messianic identity the crowd will acclaim in v.13. Faint and contested, since John explicitly redirects the act toward burial rather than coronation.

Jesus' 'you always have the poor with you' directly invokes Deut 15:11, 'the poor will never cease out of the land,' the Torah charge that grounds open-handed giving. High Volume by near-quotation and clear Availability; the allusion turns the verse's perpetual-poverty clause to relativize almsgiving against the unrepeatable burial of Messiah.

Burial anointing with spices for a king (Asa) provides OT precedent for Jesus' reading of the nard as 'for the day of my burial.' Faint; the practice is generic enough that the link rests on theme rather than verbal contact.

'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' quotes Ps 118:25-26 verbatim (hosanna = hoshia-na, 'save now'). Maximal Volume and Recurrence (a Hallel pilgrim-psalm sung at the feasts), with John adding 'the King of Israel' to make the messianic coherence explicit.

The crowd's palm branches (ta baia ton phoinikon) echo the festal foliage commanded for Booths, 'branches of palm trees,' carried in cultic rejoicing before the Lord. Coherence is strong since palms had become a nationalist-liturgical symbol of deliverance; the gesture frames Jesus' entry as covenant-festival acclamation.

'Don't be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey's colt' is a formula-cited fulfillment of Zech 9:9 (John conflates its opening with Isa/Zeph 'fear not'). Highest Volume and explicit 'as it is written'; the humble-king-on-a-colt image is the controlling typology of the whole entry.

John's 'Don't be afraid, daughter of Zion' more exactly matches Zeph 3:16 ('Do not fear, O Zion') and 3:15 ('the King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst') than Zech 9:9's 'rejoice greatly.' The 'King of Israel' acclaim (v.13) and the 'fear not' opening suggest a deliberate Zephaniah blend; medium for the conflation.

Jacob's blessing of Judah 'binding his colt (polos) to the vine' is the classic messianic donkey text read alongside Zech 9:9; the shared polos and royal-Judah expectation give faint background support to the colt motif. Low and contested: no verbal citation in John.

Simon's triumphal entry into Jerusalem 'with praise and palm branches' (also 2 Macc 10:7) shows palms as the established Second-Temple sign of liberation-procession into the holy city. Availability and Coherence make this the nearest cultural template for John's palm-waving crowd; echo, not citation.

The Greeks who 'went up to worship' and seek Jesus faintly enact the pilgrimage of the nations to Zion in the last days. Coherence with John's universalizing 'I will draw all people' (v.32) gives the motif some weight; low because no verbal contact.

The seed-sowing wisdom of 'in the morning sow your seed... you do not know which will prosper' lies behind the grain-of-wheat agricultural maxim, though Jesus inverts it: the seed must die to bear fruit. Faint and generic; sowing imagery was broadly available.

'Those who sow in tears... goes out weeping, bearing the seed... comes home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves' offers a death-to-harvest pattern resonant with the grain that dies to bear much fruit. Thematic Coherence only; no lexical anchor, hence low.

'Now my soul is troubled... save me from this time?' echoes the lament psalter, esp. Ps 6:3-4 'my soul is greatly troubled... save my life,' the Johannine analogue to the Synoptic Gethsemane. Coherence with the psalmist's troubled-soul-then-deliverance pattern is strong; medium since John gives no citation formula.

'If I am lifted up from the earth' (hypsotho) reactivates the bronze-serpent type John named in 3:14: the lifted-up serpent that gives life when looked upon prefigures the crucified-glorified Son of Man. High Coherence and Recurrence across John; the verb 'lifted up' is the load-bearing link to Moses' standard.

John's distinctive fusion of 'lifted up' with 'glorified' tracks the LXX of the Servant Song: 'my servant shall be exalted (hypsothesetai) and glorified (doxasthesetai) exceedingly.' The pairing hypsoo + doxazo is rare and precise, giving strong Volume; John reads crucifixion as the Servant's exaltation.

'Now the prince of this world will be cast out' faintly resonates with the protevangelium's defeat of the serpent. Low and contested; the casting-out of the ruler is more cosmic/apocalyptic than tied to any single verse.

The crowd's 'we have heard out of the law that the Christ remains forever' rests on the Davidic-covenant promise that his offspring/throne 'shall endure forever.' Coherence with messianic exegesis is strong; medium because John cites 'the law' generically rather than a fixed text.

'Who is this Son of Man?' and the claim that the Christ 'remains forever' invoke Daniel's heavenly Son of Man given everlasting dominion. The crowd's puzzlement over an eternal yet 'lifted up' Son of Man trades on Dan 7's title; medium for the conceptual rather than verbal link.
The notion of the messianic king whose government and reign have 'no end' supports the crowd's 'remains forever.' Faint background to the eternal-Messiah expectation; low, with no verbal contact.

'Walk while you have the light... that you may become children of light' draws on the prophetic 'walk in the light of the Lord' and the wider light/darkness covenant motif. Coherence with Isaiah's light-walking and John's pervasive light theme gives medium weight; an idiom rather than a citation.

'Lord, who has believed our report? To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?' is a formula-cited quotation ('that the word of Isaiah... might be fulfilled') of Isa 53:1 LXX verbatim. Maximal Volume; John reads Israel's unbelief at the signs through the Servant Song's lament over a rejected revelation.

'He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they should see... and turn, and I would heal them' quotes Isa 6:10, the commission-text of judicial hardening (cf. its NT recurrence). High Volume and explicit attribution to Isaiah; the divine blinding explains the unbelief just described.

'Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him' alludes to the throne-vision of Isa 6:1, 'I saw the Lord... high and lifted up,' identifying the glory Isaiah beheld with Christ's. Strong Coherence: John binds the 'lifted up' (hypsoo) Servant to the 'high and lifted up' enthroned Lord of the call narrative.

'I spoke not from myself, but the Father... gave me a commandment what I should say' and the warning that the rejected 'word' will judge in the last day echo the prophet-like-Moses who speaks only the words God commands, and whom God will hold men accountable to hear. Coherence with John's prophet christology is strong; medium absent a citation formula.

'I know that his commandment is eternal life... this word is your life' resonates with Moses' charge that the law-word 'is no trifle for you, but your very life.' Faint thematic link between commandment and life; low, with only conceptual contact.

'I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes... may not remain in the darkness' continues the light-to-the-nations motif of Isaiah's eschatological dawn. Coherence with John's universal-light christology gives faint support; low, idiomatic rather than cited.
